4|Androgen-deprivation therapy alone or with docetaxel in
5|non-castrate metastatic prostate cancer (GETUG-AFU 15):
6|a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial
7|Gwenaelle Gravis, Karim Fizazi, Florence Joly, Stéphane Oudard, Franck Priou, Benjamin Esterni, Igor Latorzeff , Remy Delva, Ivan Krakowski,
8|Brigitte Laguerre, Fréderic Rolland, Christine Théodore, Gael Deplanque, Jean Marc Ferrero, Damien Pouessel, Loïc Mourey, Philippe Beuzeboc,
9|Sylvie Zanetta, Muriel Habibian, Jean François Berdah, Jerome Dauba, Marjorie Baciuchka, Christian Platini, Claude Linassier, Jean Luc Labourey,
10|Jean Pascal Machiels, Claude El Kouri, Alain Ravaud, Etienne Suc, Jean Christophe Eymard, Ali Hasbini, Guilhem Bousquet, Michel Soulie
11|Summary
12|Background Early chemotherapy might improve the overall outcomes of patients with metastatic non-castrate (ie,
13|hormone-sensitive) prostate cancer. We investigated the eff ects of the addition of docetaxel to androgen-deprivation
14|therapy (ADT) for patients with metastatic non-castrate prostate cancer.
15|Methods In this randomised, open-label, phase 3 study, we enrolled patients in 29 centres in France and one in
16|Belgium. Eligible patients were older than 18 years and had histologically confi rmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate
17|and radiologically proven metastatic disease; a Karnofsky score of at least 70%; a life expectancy of at least 3 months;
18|and adequate hepatic, haematological, and renal function. They were randomly assigned to receive to ADT (orchiectomy
19|or luteinising hormone-releasing hormone agonists, alone or combined with non-steroidal antiandrogens) alone or in
20|combination with docetaxel (75 mg/m2 intravenously on the fi rst day of each 21-day cycle; up to nine cycles). Patients
21|were randomised in a 1:1 ratio, with dynamic minimisation to minimise imbalances in previous systemic treatment
22|with ADT, chemotherapy for local disease or isolated rising concentration of serum prostate-specifi c antigen, and
23|Glass risk groups. Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not masked to treatment allocation. The primary
24|endpoint was overall survival. Effi cacy analyses were done by intention to treat. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.
25|gov, number NCT00104715.
26|Findings Between Oct 18, 2004, and Dec 31, 2008, 192 patients were randomly allocated to receive ADT plus docetaxel
27|and 193 to receive ADT alone. Median follow-up was 50 months (IQR 39-63). Median overall survival was 58·9 months
28|(95% CI 50·8-69·1) in the group given ADT plus docetaxel and 54·2 months (42·2-not reached) in that given ADT
29|alone (hazard ratio 1·01, 95% CI 0·75-1·36). 72 serious adverse events were reported in the group given ADT plus
30|docetaxel, of which the most frequent were neutropenia (40 [21%]), febrile neutropenia (six [3%]), abnormal liver
31|function tests (three [2%]), and neutropenia with infection (two [1%]). Four treatment-related deaths occurred in the
32|ADT plus docetaxel group (two of which were neutropenia-related), after which the data monitoring committee
33|recommended treatment with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. After this recommendation, no further
34|treatment-related deaths occurred. No serious adverse events were reported in the ADT alone group.
35|Interpretation Docetaxel should not be used as part of fi rst-line treatment for patients with non-castrate metastatic
36|prostate cancer.
37|Funding French Health Ministry and Institut National du Cancer (PHRC), Sanofi -Aventis, AstraZeneca, and Amgen.
38|Introduction
39|Worldwide, prostate cancer is the second most common
40|malignancy1 and is the third most common cause of
41|cancer death in men in developed countries.2 Metastases
42|are rare at the time of diagnosis-at least in developed
43|countries3-but can eventually develop after failure of
44|local
45|treatment.
46|Bi lateral
47|orchiectomy
48|(medical
49|castration) is recommended for initial treatment of non-
50|castrate (ie, hormone-sensitive) metastatic prostate
51|cancer.4,5 Median duration of sensitivity to androgen-
52|deprivation therapy (ADT) is usually 24-36 months;6
53|before new active drugs were introduced, median
54|survival was about 30 months (95% CI 12-53).7 However,
55|the outcome of this treatment varies widely. A set of
56|prognostic groups was developed that separated patients
57|on the basis of appendicular versus axial disease, an
58|Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status
59|of 0 versus 1-3, concen tration of prostate-specifi c antigen
60|(PSA) of less than 65 ng/mL versus 65 ng/mL or more,
61|and a Gleason score less than 8 versus 8 or more.8 With
62|these criteria, three groups were identifi ed: good (42% of
63|patients survive to 5 years), intermediate (21%), and poor
64|(9%) prognosis.8
65|Metastatic prostate cancer eventually becomes resistant
66|to castration. Until 2004, docetaxel with prednisone was
67|the only treatment that could improve survival.9,10 The
68|benefi t of these drugs in castration-resistant prostate
69|cancer suggested that early chemotherapy might improve

4|the overall outcome of patients with metastatic non-
5|castrate prostate cancer. Thus, we aimed to assess the
6|effi cacy and safety of docetaxel combined with ADT
7|versus ADT alone in patients with metastatic non-
8|castrate prostate cancer.
9|Methods
10|Participants
11|In this randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial, we enrolled
12|participants from 29 centres in France and one in
13|Belgium. Indi viduals aged more than 18 years were
14|eligible if they had histologically confi rmed adeno-
15|carcinoma of the prostate and radiologically proven
16|metastatic disease; a Karnofsky score of at least 70%; a life
17|expectancy of at least 3 months; and adequate hepatic,
18|haematological, and renal func tion. Patients who had
19|received previous chemotherapy for metastatic disease
20|were excluded, but ADT for patients with metastatic
21|disease could have been initiated no more than 2 months
22|before enrolment. In the neo adjuvant and adjuvant
23|settings or in the context of isolated PSA increase, previous
24|chemo therapy or ADT, or both, were allowed, with the
25|condition that the treatment had been discontinued at
26|least 12 months before inclusion in the study and no
27|metastases or PSA increase had been documented during
28|this period. Radiotherapy for metastatic disease was to be
29|completed at least 4 weeks before enrolment.
30|Patients were excluded from study entry when they had
31|severe cardiac disease, had had surgical castration before
32|metastatic disease occurred, had evidence of brain
33|metastasis, had peripheral neuropathy (at least grade 2),
34|a history of another cancer in the past 5 years (except
35|basal-cell or squamous-cell skin cancer), or another
36|serious condition that could jeopardise their participation.
37|The protocol was reviewed by the internal review
38|boards of all participating institutions and the study
39|was approved by a central national ethics committee. The
40|study was done in accordance with Good Clinical Practice
41|guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients
42|provided written informed consent.
43|Randomisation and masking
44|Randomisation was done by a clinical research organ-
45|isation and was centralised nationally. Patients were
46|randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive ADT plus
47|docetaxel or ADT alone. Dynamic minimisation was
48|used to minimise the imbalance of three criteria:
49|previous systemic treatment with ADT; chemotherapy
50|for local disease or isolated rising PSA; and Glass risk
51|groups.8 Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not
52|masked to treatment allocation.
53|Procedures
54|All patients received ADT, which consisted of orchi ectomy
55|or luteinising hormone-releasing hormone agonists,
56|alone or combined with non-steroidal antiandrogens.
57|ADT was given continuously until unaccept able toxic
58|eff ects or discontinuation on patients' request. In the
59|group given ADT plus docetaxel, patients received
60|75 mg/m2 intravenous docetaxel in a 250 cm3 5% glucose
61|solution in the course of 1 h on the fi rst day of each 21-day
62|cycle. Treatment with docetaxel continued for up to nine
63|cycles on the basis of the median exposure reported in the
64|TAX 327 trial,9 or was discontinued prematurely in the
65|case of progression, unacceptable toxic eff ects, or patients'
66|request. Premedication with a corticosteroid (8 mg
67|dexamethasone or equivalent) was given orally in the
68|evening before the infusion of docetaxel, on the day of
69|docetaxel infusion, and on the next day.
70|If predefi ned toxic eff ects occurred (haematological or
71|non-haematological eff ects; gastrointestinal, skin, and
72|liver toxic eff ects; peripheral neuropathy; or docetaxel-
73|specifi c adverse events), docetaxel could be delayed until
74|recovery or the dose could be reduced by up to 25%.
75|Bisphosphonates were allowed with fi rst-line treatment.
76|We assessed clinical history, weight, and Karnofsky
77|performance status, and did a physical examination
78|before treatment began. We did a CT scan, a bone scan,
79|electrocardiography, and blood tests (including meas ure-
80|ment of serum PSA) within 30 days before initiation of
81|treatment. We repeated physical examinations and blood
82|tests every 3 weeks during treatment in the group given
83|ADT plus docetaxel and every 3 months in the group
84|given ADT alone. We did imaging studies every 3 months;
85|radiological response was to be confi rmed within
86|4 weeks. After 42 months, we did clinical, labora tory, and
87|radiological examinations every 6 months.
88|The primary endpoint was overall survival (ie, time
89|between randomisation and death from any cause).
90|Secondary endpoints were time to clinical progression or
91|death (clinical progression-free survival; cPFS) and time
92|to PSA progression, clinical progression, or death
93|(biochemical progression-free survival; bPFS).
94|We defi ned biochemical progression with the PSA
95|Working Group defi nition:11 a previous confi rmed PSA
96|decrease of at least 50% and an increase of at least 50%
97|above the nadir, with a minimum increase of 5 ng/mL.
98|For patients without a previous PSA decrease of 50%,
99|progression was defi ned as a PSA increase of at least
100|25% above the nadir and of at least 5 ng/mL.
101|A confi rmatory PSA test was mandatory in all cases.
102|In patients with measurable lesions, we defi ned clinical
103|progression as the progression of pre-existing lesions
104|with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors
105|(RECIST; version 1.0)12 or the occurrence of (new) bone
106|lesions, whichever happened fi rst. In patients with only
107|bone lesions, progression was defi ned as one or more
108|new bone lesions on bone scan or occurrence of a new
109|soft-tissue lesion, whichever happened fi rst. Death was
110|judged as an event; causes of deaths were reported by
111|investigators rather than by central review.
112|We assessed adverse events with the Common Toxicity
113|Criteria of the National Cancer Institute (version 3).

6|pleted the questionnaire at initiation, 3 months, and
7|6 months, and then subsequently twice a year.
8|Statistical analysis
9|The planned sample of 378 patients provided 80% power
10|to detect a hazard ratio (HR) of 0·62 for death in the
11|group receiving ADT plus docetaxel as compared with
12|that receiving ADT alone. We calculated this sample size
13|with the assumption that 65% of the group given ADT
14|plus docetaxel and 50% of the group given ADT alone
15|would survive to 36 months,7,8,13 with a two-sided α of
16|0·05 and a fi xed 36-month follow-up period to record the
17|146 necessary events. Initially, the study was planned
18|with only 36 months of follow-up for all patients. To
19|reach the number of necessary events, the sponsor
20|decided to follow up all enrolled patients until one cutoff
21|date, namely July 31, 2011. Patients with no event at the
22|last visit or on July 31, 2011, were censored.
23|We did the effi cacy analyses by intention to treat. Safety
24|analyses were based on the population exposed to the
25|assigned treatment. We did post-hoc subgroup analyses
26|to assess whether specifi c baseline characteristics
27|aff ected overall survival and bPFS. We estimated
28|distributions of time-to-event variables and associated
29|95% CIs with the Kaplan-Meier product-limit method.
30|The log-rank test was the primary analysis for comparison
31|of treat ment groups. We estimated adjusted and
32|unadjusted treatment eff ects with the Cox proportional-
33|hazards model. Because PSA progression is a time-
34|dependent covariate, we used a 7-month landmark
35|analysis to investigate its eff ect on overall survival. We
36|chose to do a landmark analysis with bPFS because cPFS
37|is diffi cult to assess in metastatic prostate cancer and
38|bPFS was considered to be more specifi c than is cPFS.
39|We chose 7 months to compare our results with those of
40|the landmark analysis of Hussain and colleagues.14
41|We estimated follow-up with the reverse censoring
42|method and time to subsequent treatments with standard
43|descriptive median on the restricted population who
44|received at least one treatment. We tested the proportional
45|hazard assumption with the Grambsch and Therneau
46|method.15 Other statistical inferences were assessed with
47|the χ2 statistic. All statistical analyses were done with
48|R (version 2.15.1).
49|This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number
50|NCT00104715.
51|Role of the funding source
52|The sponsors of the study had no role in study design,
53|data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or
54|writing of the report. Raw data was the property of
55|UNICANCER, and all authors could access the data by
56|request to UNICANCER and the corresponding author.
57|UNICANCER and GG had fi nal responsibility for the
58|decision to submit for publication.

4|patients developed metastases after local treatment.
5|Metastatic sites were mainly bone, nodes, and lungs
6|(table 1). Metastases in extrapelvic nodes were reported in
7|only 55 (14%) patients. No patients were lost to follow-up.
8|One patient in the group assigned to receive ADT alone
9|received docetaxel and was included in the group given
10|ADT plus docetaxel for the safety analyses (fi gure 1).
11|ADT was started between 15 days and 2 months before
12|randomisation in roughly half the patients (table 1). In
13|the group given ADT plus docetaxel, castration was
14|obtained with luteinising hormone-releasing hormone
15|agonists alone in 67 patients (35%) and with combined
16|blockade in 123 patients (64%; two patients did not
17|receive ADT because consent withdrawn). In the group
18|given ADT alone, luteinising hormone-releasing hor-
19|mone alone was used in 59 patients (31%) and combined
20|blockade in 131 patients (68%; three patients did not
21|receive ADT because consent withdrawn).
22|The median number of docetaxel cycles was eight
23|(range zero to nine); 93 patients (48%) received the nine
24|planned cycles. Doses were reduced in 21 (11%) of the 189
25|patients who received docetaxel. Of the 99 patients who
26|discontinued docetaxel, 39 did so due to toxic eff ects, six
27|due to disease pro gression, two due to protocol violations,
28|and 52 for other reasons.
29|120 (62%) of the 193 patients allocated to receive ADT
30|alone subsequently received docetaxel at the time of
31|progression of castration-resistant prostate cancer and
32|54 (28%) of the 192 patients allocated to receive ADT plus
33|docetaxel were rechallenged with docetaxel at the time of
34|progression to castration resistance. The median length
35|of time from randomisation to subsequent chemotherapy
36|was 16 months (IQR 10-24) in the group given ADT
37|alone versus 26 months (18-36) in the group given ADT
38|plus docetaxel.
39|After progression, some patients received other
40|treatments that could have aff ected survival (table 2).
41|First-line bisphosphonates were given to 34 patients
42|(18%) in the group given ADT plus docetaxel and
43|25 (13%) in that given ADT alone (p=0·25).
44|Median follow-up was 50 months (IQR 39-63). At the
45|cutoff date (July 31, 2011), 176 patients-88 (46%) in
46|each group-had died (fi gure 1). Causes of death were
47|disease progression (68 [77%] in the group given ADT
48|plus docetaxel; 75 [85%] in the group given ADT alone),
49|treatment-related toxic eff ects (two [2%; none), other
50|cancers (fi ve [6%]; none), other reasons (fi ve [6%]; six
51|[7%]), and unknown reasons (eight [9%]; seven [8%]).
52|Subsequent UNICANCER review deemed that four
53|deaths (5%) in the group given ADT plus docetaxel were
54|treatment-related; one death had previously been
55|thought to be due to progressive disease, but no
56|information was available for the other additional
57|treatment-related death.
58|Median overall survival was 58·9 months (95% CI
59|50·8-69·1) in the group given ADT plus docetaxel and
60|54·2 months (42·2-not reached) in the group given ADT
61|alone (HR 1·01, 95% CI 0·75-1·36; p=0·955; fi gure 2).

4|Discussion
5|We have shown that the combin ation of ADT plus
6|docetaxel in patients with metastatic non-castrate
7|prostate cancer did not signifi cantly in crease overall
8|survival compared with ADT alone.
9|Overall survival is deemed to be the best endpoint to
10|assess the outcome of anticancer treatments-especially
11|in prostate cancer-because response and progression of
12|bone metastases is often diffi cult to measure and the value
13|of PSA as a surrogate endpoint is controversial. In our
14|study, the absence of a diff erence between groups probably
15|cannot be explained by insuffi cient follow-up duration,
16|because we did not record even a slight benefi cial eff ect of
17|chemotherapy. However, overall survival was aff ected by
18|crossover treatments: in our study, almost two-thirds of
19|patients assigned to receive ADT alone were given
20|docetaxel at the time of castration-resistant prostate cancer
21|progression, but just over a quarter of those assigned to
22|receive ADT plus docetaxel received additional docetaxel-
23|based chemotherapy, which potentially confounded
24|detection of a treatment-related survival benefi t.
25|We did show improvements with ADT plus docetaxel in
26|all effi cacy secondary endpoints, such as PSA in crease,
27|bPFS, and cPFS. The discrepancies between bPFS and
28|time to subsequent treatment were due to the diff erent
29|esti mation methods. Because we obtained relevant infor-
30|mation only if a new treatment was reported, we estimated
31|the median time to new treatment only in patients who
32|received a new treatment. We estimated other median
33|survival measures (bPFS, cPFS) with the Kaplan-Meier
34|method and censored times for patients without events.
35|Median bPFS and cPFS in populations restricted to
36|individuals with a documented new treatment were lower
37|than in the whole population (18 months and 19 months
38|in the group given ADT plus docetaxel; 11 months and
39|12 months in the group given ADT alone).
40|The secondary endpoints are clinically relevant. Early PSA
41|progression (an increase of ≥25%) within the fi rst 6 months
42|of treatment correlates with overall survival in both non-
43|castrate and castration-resistant prostate can cer.17 The
44|analysis18 of the TAX 327 study of patients with metastatic
45|castration-resistant prostate cancer showed that PSA
46|response (ie, at least 50% reduction in serum PSA from
47|baseline that was maintained for at least 3 weeks) was
48|associated with longer survival. Final results of the S9346
49|study19 showed that median overall survival was 3·6 years

8|Notably, we showed that the progression-hazards model
9|was not proportional (whether biochemical or clinical),
10|with a decrease in the benefi cial eff ect of chemotherapy
11|with time; therefore, docetaxel effi cacy dimin ishes before
12|progression occurs. This fi nding could partly explain the
13|absence of a diff erence in overall survival between the two
14|groups, despite the short-term effi cacy of chemotherapy
15|in terms of biological variables.
16|Median overall survival in our study was longer than
17|that previously reported in patients with metastatic
18|non-castrate prostate cancer treated with ADT,19,20 which is
19|another possible explanation for the absence of survival
20|diff erence between the two groups. Our initial hypothesis
21|was that we would record a median survival of 3 years in
22|the group given ADT alone on the basis of previous
23|reports, but median survival in our cohort was longer than
24|expected (54·2 months [4·5 years]). Our patients might
25|have been diagnosed earlier in their history of metastatic
26|disease than have others, because PSA measurement and
27|im proved imaging techniques are now frequently used. In
28|a previous study,20 survival was diff erent between cohorts
29|included at diff erent periods; median survival was
30|33 months in S8894 (patients included from 1989 to 1994)
31|and 49 months in S9346 (patients included from 1995 to
32|2009). Additionally, an increased prevalence of widespread
33|disease and bone pain and substantially higher PSA
34|concentrations were recorded in early trials.20
35|Diff erences in survival between our study and others
36|persist in the subgroup analysis. In the study by Glass
37|and colleagues,8 median overall survival was 54 months in
38|the good-prognosis group, 30 months in the intermediate-
39|prognosis group, and 21 months in the poor-prognosis
40|group-ie, all shorter than in our trial. Longer survival in
41|our study could be due to improved treatment in
42|metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer or stage
43|migration in patients with metastatic disease. However,
44|most participants in our trial had bone or visceral
45|metastases (few had isolated node involvement).
46|Therefore, several possible reasons exist for the absence
47|of a diff erence in overall survival between the two groups
48|in our study. First, docetaxel does not confer benefi ts in
49|metastatic non-castrate prostate cancer, or alternatively
50|docetaxel has a decreasing eff ect on progression-free
51|survival that does not confer advantages in terms of
52|overall survival. Second, we might not have calculated an
53|appropriate sample size, because survival duration might
54|have been underestimated for the group given ADT alone
55|and diff erence in the group given ADT plus docetaxel
56|overestimated. Third, crossover to docetaxel at the time of
57|progression might have had an eff ect.
58|Very few studies and no phase 3 trials have assessed
59|the combination of docetaxel-based chemotherapy and
60|ADT in metastatic non-castrate prostate cancer (panel).
61|Millikan and colleagues21 included 286 patients and
62|compared ketoconazole and doxorubicin alternating with
63|vinblastine and estramustine given with ADT versus
64|standard ADT. They recorded no signifi cant diff erences
65|in time to progression of castration-resistant prostate
66|cancer and in median survival between the two groups.21
67|A study by Wang and coworkers22 compared the com-
68|bination of mitoxantrone and ADT with ADT alone in
69|93 patients with locally advanced (n=38) or metastatic
70|(n=55) prostate cancer. Overall survival and responses
71|were signifi cantly improved in patients with locally
72|advanced disease given mitoxantrone, but patients with
73|metastatic disease did not benefi t.
74|Some studies have investigated the addition of
75|chemotherapy to ADT in early-stage prostate cancers.
76|The preliminary results of the GETUG 12 phase 3 study,23
77|which compared ADT alone and ADT plus docetaxel and
78|estramustine in high-risk prostate cancers treated locally
79|mainly by radiotherapy, showed that PSA response was
80|signifi cantly higher in the group given chemotherapy
81|than in that given ADT alone, but long-term data are not
82|available yet. The results of the SWOG S9921 study,24
83|which compared ADT alone or in combination with
84|mitoxantrone as adjuvant therapy in high-risk men who

6|Discontinuation of docetaxel in our study was mainly
7|because of toxic eff ects. In the TAX 327 study,9 a smaller
8|proportion of patients (11%) treated with docetaxel every

10|than in our study. However, a proportion similar to that

13|(22%) in the CALGB 90401 phase 3 study.25
14|Our data show that adverse events after docetaxel
15|treatment should be closely monitored, and the frequency
16|of severe neutropenia should be limited by granulocyte
17|colony-stimulating factor. Before the amend ment of the
18|study protocol to allow administration of granulocyte
19|colony-stimulating factor, grade 3-5 neutro penia was
20|noted in almost a third of patients, 7% of patients had
21|febrile neutropenia, and two patients died from
22|neutropenia-related conditions. However, after the amend-
23|ment, the frequency of neutropenia and febrile neutropenia
24|of grade 3-4 decreased substantially and no subsequent
25|toxic deaths occurred. Febrile neutropenia after docetaxel
26|treatment was more frequent in our study than in previous
27|trials of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (3%
28|in TAX 3279 and 4·2% in CALGB 9040125) or in the
29|neoadjuvant setting in high-risk localised prostate cancers
30|(2% in GETUG 1222). Previous reports26-28 have suggested
31|that the frequency of severe neutropenia is reduced in
32|castration-resistant prostate cancer compared with non-
33|castrate prostate or non-prostate cancer. This fi nding
34|might be explained by a decreased docetaxel exposure in
35|metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer:29 Docetaxel
36|clearance is in creased by about 100% in men with
37|castration-resistant prostate cancer compared with those
38|with non-castrate disease, and is associated with a two-fold
39|reduction in the area under the curve, although hepatic
40|activity of cytochrome P450 3A4 is unchanged (p=0·0001),
41|probably because of an increase in hepatocyte uptake.
42|Our study has limitations. We might not have had
43|suffi cient power to show a small diff erence in overall
44|survival-if any-because we underestimated overall
45|survival in the ADT group, and were overoptimistic in
46|terms of potential diff erence in survival when we did our
47|sample size calculation. Additionally, we do not have
48|information about response to docetaxel (either fi rst
49|docetaxel treatment for patients previously treated with
50|ADT alone or rechallenge in those who had received
51|ADT plus docetaxel).
52|In summary, we showed that the addition of chemo-
53|therapy to ADT does not provide a benefi t in terms of
54|overall survival compared with ADT alone, although
55|bPFS, cPFS, and PSA response were improved. Although
56|quality of life was impaired during docetaxel treatment,
57|global scores at 12 months were generally similar in the
58|two groups. Overall, our results suggest that docetaxel
59|should not be added to ADT in fi rst-line treatment for
60|metastatic non-castrate prostate cancer.

89|Systematic review
90|We searched Medline and PubMed for reports published in
91|English or French between Jan 1, 1994, and June 1, 2004, with
92|the search terms "prostate cancer", "metastatic prostate
93|cancer", "hormone sensitive prostate cancer", "castrate", "non
94|castrate", "androgen deprivation therapy", "chemotherapy",
95|"docetaxel", "hormone resistance", "castrate resistance",
96|"phase III", and "randomized study". We assessed the quality
97|of evidence by methods used, with the highest quality
98|attributed to randomised studies. We identifi ed two
99|randomised trials9,10 that showed that chemotherapy-namely
100|docetaxel-could improve survival in patients with metastatic
101|castration-resistant prostate cancer. Additionally, we identifi ed
102|11 randomised trials of castration with or without
103|chemotherapy other than docetaxel in patients with metastatic
104|non-castrate (ie, hormone-sensitive) prostate cancer. None of
105|these trials showed improvement in survival. We obtained
106|up-to-date information from abstracts and congress
107|presentations on Current Contents and Web of Science.

109|from the Physician Data Query NCI's list of cancer clinical trials.

111|As far as we are aware, ours is the fi rst phase 3 trial to have
112|assessed docetaxel chemotherapy in patients with metastatic
113|non-castrate prostate cancer. As has been previously
114|described with other cytotoxic drugs, the addition of
115|docetaxel to androgen-deprivation therapy did not improve
116|survival compared with androgen-deprivation therapy alone
117|in metastatic non-castrate prostate cancer in our study.

result.relation_rationale: The report labels its secondary endpoint cPFS and defines it as time to clinical progression or death, measured from randomization. The lesion-specific progression criteria include RECIST 1.0 progression of pre-existing measurable lesions or new bone lesions and a separate definition for bone-only disease. Death is an event. The report compares the two randomized groups using the intention-to-treat population and reports the cPFS hazard ratio.

measurement.method: Clinical progression-free survival: time to clinical progression or death. Clinical progression was progression of pre-existing measurable lesions by RECIST version 1.0 or new bone lesions, whichever occurred first; for bone-only disease, one or more new bone lesions or a new soft-tissue lesion, whichever occurred first.

time_point_or_window.description: From randomization until clinical progression or death; patients without an event were censored at last visit or July 31, 2011.

target.intended_analysis_population: All randomized participants in the comparison groups

reported.analysis_population: Intention-to-treat population: 192 patients allocated to ADT plus docetaxel and 193 allocated to ADT alone; no patients were lost to follow-up.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.

questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

evidence.quote:
We assessed clinical history, weight, and Karnofsky
performance status, and did a physical examination
before treatment began. We did a CT scan, a bone scan,
electrocardiography, and blood tests (including meas ure-
ment of serum PSA) within 30 days before initiation of
treatment. We repeated physical examinations and blood
tests every 3 weeks during treatment in the group given
ADT plus docetaxel and every 3 months in the group
given ADT alone. We did imaging studies every 3 months;
radiological response was to be confi rmed within
4 weeks. After 42 months, we did clinical, labora tory, and
radiological examinations every 6 months.
The primary endpoint was overall survival (ie, time
between randomisation and death from any cause).
Secondary endpoints were time to clinical progression or
death (clinical progression-free survival; cPFS) and time
to PSA progression, clinical progression, or death
(biochemical progression-free survival; bPFS).
We defi ned biochemical progression with the PSA
Working Group defi nition:11 a previous confi rmed PSA
decrease of at least 50% and an increase of at least 50%
above the nadir, with a minimum increase of 5 ng/mL.
For patients without a previous PSA decrease of 50%,
progression was defi ned as a PSA increase of at least
25% above the nadir and of at least 5 ng/mL.
A confi rmatory PSA test was mandatory in all cases.
In patients with measurable lesions, we defi ned clinical
progression as the progression of pre-existing lesions
with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors
(RECIST; version 1.0)12 or the occurrence of (new) bone
lesions, whichever happened fi rst. In patients with only
bone lesions, progression was defi ned as one or more
new bone lesions on bone scan or occurrence of a new
soft-tissue lesion, whichever happened fi rst. Death was
judged as an event; causes of deaths were reported by
investigators rather than by central review.

evidence.quote:
patients developed metastases after local treatment.
Metastatic sites were mainly bone, nodes, and lungs
(table 1). Metastases in extrapelvic nodes were reported in
only 55 (14%) patients. No patients were lost to follow-up.
One patient in the group assigned to receive ADT alone

Randomisation and masking
Randomisation was done by a clinical research organ-
isation and was centralised nationally. Patients were
randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive ADT plus
docetaxel or ADT alone. Dynamic minimisation was
used to minimise the imbalance of three criteria:
previous systemic treatment with ADT; chemotherapy
for local disease or isolated rising PSA; and Glass risk
groups.8 Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not
masked to treatment allocation.

Methods In this randomised, open-label, phase 3 study, we enrolled patients in 29 centres in France and one in
Belgium. Eligible patients were older than 18 years and had histologically confi rmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate
and radiologically proven metastatic disease; a Karnofsky score of at least 70%; a life expectancy of at least 3 months;
and adequate hepatic, haematological, and renal function. They were randomly assigned to receive to ADT (orchiectomy
or luteinising hormone-releasing hormone agonists, alone or combined with non-steroidal antiandrogens) alone or in
combination with docetaxel (75 mg/m2 intravenously on the fi rst day of each 21-day cycle; up to nine cycles). Patients
were randomised in a 1:1 ratio, with dynamic minimisation to minimise imbalances in previous systemic treatment
with ADT, chemotherapy for local disease or isolated rising concentration of serum prostate-specifi c antigen, and
Glass risk groups. Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not masked to treatment allocation. The primary
endpoint was overall survival. Effi cacy analyses were done by intention to treat. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.
gov, number NCT00104715.

Median bPFS was signifi cantly longer in the group
given ADT plus docetaxel (22·9 months, 95% CI
19·6-28·4) than in the group given ADT alone
(12·9 months, 11·9-17·7; HR 0·72, 0·57-0·91; p=0·005;
fi gure 3). Similarly, median cPFS was signifi cantly longer
in the group given ADT plus docetaxel (23·5 months,
20·5-31·9) than in the group given ADT alone

result.relation_rationale: The report labels its secondary endpoint cPFS and defines it as time to clinical progression or death, measured from randomization. The lesion-specific progression criteria include RECIST 1.0 progression of pre-existing measurable lesions or new bone lesions and a separate definition for bone-only disease. Death is an event. The report compares the two randomized groups using the intention-to-treat population and reports the cPFS hazard ratio.

measurement.method: Clinical progression-free survival: time to clinical progression or death. Clinical progression was progression of pre-existing measurable lesions by RECIST version 1.0 or new bone lesions, whichever occurred first; for bone-only disease, one or more new bone lesions or a new soft-tissue lesion, whichever occurred first.

time_point_or_window.description: From randomization until clinical progression or death; patients without an event were censored at last visit or July 31, 2011.

questions.wording: Were participants aware of their assigned intervention during the trial?
questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 28, Box 6, signalling question 2.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

evidence.quote:
We assessed clinical history, weight, and Karnofsky
performance status, and did a physical examination
before treatment began. We did a CT scan, a bone scan,
electrocardiography, and blood tests (including meas ure-
ment of serum PSA) within 30 days before initiation of
treatment. We repeated physical examinations and blood
tests every 3 weeks during treatment in the group given
ADT plus docetaxel and every 3 months in the group
given ADT alone. We did imaging studies every 3 months;
radiological response was to be confi rmed within
4 weeks. After 42 months, we did clinical, labora tory, and
radiological examinations every 6 months.
The primary endpoint was overall survival (ie, time
between randomisation and death from any cause).
Secondary endpoints were time to clinical progression or
death (clinical progression-free survival; cPFS) and time
to PSA progression, clinical progression, or death
(biochemical progression-free survival; bPFS).
We defi ned biochemical progression with the PSA
Working Group defi nition:11 a previous confi rmed PSA
decrease of at least 50% and an increase of at least 50%
above the nadir, with a minimum increase of 5 ng/mL.
For patients without a previous PSA decrease of 50%,
progression was defi ned as a PSA increase of at least
25% above the nadir and of at least 5 ng/mL.
A confi rmatory PSA test was mandatory in all cases.
In patients with measurable lesions, we defi ned clinical
progression as the progression of pre-existing lesions
with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors
(RECIST; version 1.0)12 or the occurrence of (new) bone
lesions, whichever happened fi rst. In patients with only
bone lesions, progression was defi ned as one or more
new bone lesions on bone scan or occurrence of a new
soft-tissue lesion, whichever happened fi rst. Death was
judged as an event; causes of deaths were reported by
investigators rather than by central review.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.

A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether an appropriate analysis estimated the effect of assignment to intervention. Compare randomized assignment with the actual analysis population, grouping, reassignment, and exclusions, including their reasons; an ITT, modified ITT, or as-treated label alone does not establish this.
considerations: The question is about effect of assignment, so grouping must follow randomized assignment.
Assess what the analysis actually did, not the label attached to it: ITT/mITT/as-treated terminology is a description to verify against assignment, grouping, and exclusions.

Never-treated participants are not automatically participants with no adverse event or unavailable outcome. Recover the documented eligibility, outcome availability, and exclusion reason before judging the approved assignment-effect estimand.

A post-randomization exclusion of an eligible participant remains an analysis concern whether it happened before the endpoint was measured or after an outcome value was recorded. Record that timing separately: an outcome not collected may also matter to D3, while an observed value omitted from the assignment analysis is not thereby missing outcome data. Judge 2.7 from the excluded participants, reasons, outcome rarity, and prognostic relevance for this Result.
questions.decision_rule: Consider ITT and modified ITT excluding participants with missing outcome data appropriate. The lesion-specific progression criteria include RECIST 1.0 progression of pre-existing measurable lesions or new bone lesions and a separate definition for bone-only disease. Death is an event. The report compares the two randomized groups using the intention-to-treat population and reports the cPFS hazard ratio.

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When the extent remains unknown, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the extent of missing outcome data remains unknown after bounded retrieval. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Neutral paired control: complete ascertainment and an analysis denominator with unresolved ascertainment differ only in the availability premise; administrative censoring and worsening-related follow-up loss differ only in the missingness mechanism.

evidence.quote:
We assessed clinical history, weight, and Karnofsky
performance status, and did a physical examination
before treatment began. We did a CT scan, a bone scan,
electrocardiography, and blood tests (including meas ure-
ment of serum PSA) within 30 days before initiation of
treatment. We repeated physical examinations and blood
tests every 3 weeks during treatment in the group given
ADT plus docetaxel and every 3 months in the group
given ADT alone. We did imaging studies every 3 months;
radiological response was to be confi rmed within
4 weeks. After 42 months, we did clinical, labora tory, and
radiological examinations every 6 months.
The primary endpoint was overall survival (ie, time
between randomisation and death from any cause).
Secondary endpoints were time to clinical progression or
death (clinical progression-free survival; cPFS) and time
to PSA progression, clinical progression, or death
(biochemical progression-free survival; bPFS).
We defi ned biochemical progression with the PSA
Working Group defi nition:11 a previous confi rmed PSA
decrease of at least 50% and an increase of at least 50%
above the nadir, with a minimum increase of 5 ng/mL.
For patients without a previous PSA decrease of 50%,
progression was defi ned as a PSA increase of at least
25% above the nadir and of at least 5 ng/mL.
A confi rmatory PSA test was mandatory in all cases.
In patients with measurable lesions, we defi ned clinical
progression as the progression of pre-existing lesions
with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors
(RECIST; version 1.0)12 or the occurrence of (new) bone
lesions, whichever happened fi rst. In patients with only
bone lesions, progression was defi ned as one or more
new bone lesions on bone scan or occurrence of a new
soft-tissue lesion, whichever happened fi rst. Death was
judged as an event; causes of deaths were reported by
investigators rather than by central review.

guidance: Answer every initially active question plus each dependent question whose activation predicate is met by your earlier answers. Extra inactive branch answers are ignored and never committed. Preserve the approved Result target.

Evaluate activated questions in question order. Submit every activated question with a justification, unknowns, and counterevidence. Review the inspected passages against its exact proposition and check material contradictions. Reuse adequate Evidence. When a premise remains unresolved, state the unresolved premise and why you stopped, and use bounded discovery across relevant Sources, including a protocol or SAP when relevant. Inspect returned passages before using them. A limitation requires that explicit premise and stopping rationale; include a Trial-scoped search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful, but a direct read does not require a search receipt. Absence requires a scoped untruncated no-hit receipt.

Cite complete premises for the active question. One passage may support several facts. When an answer depends on separate passages, cite each with its own boundaries. A relationship kind describes the use of Evidence; it adds no scientific fact.

When inference, conflict, or uncertainty connects Evidence to an answer, include a concise question-specific justification. State what the passages establish, what remains unresolved, and why the selected option follows. Any support relationship is host-asserted: the server checks structure, ownership, and exact Evidence provenance but does not independently judge semantic entailment.

Working premise records are source-grounded resumable notes. Reuse them only when the working checkpoint is current for this exact approved Result and captured Source projection; a stale checkpoint requires the stated recovery action and never carries a prior Domain judgment into this assessment.
A definitive yes or no needs direct_support, indirect_support, or contradiction; a limitation or absence alone supports uncertainty, not a definitive answer.

Evaluate activation against your draft answers. If validation reports missing active question IDs, add those questions with allowed answer values and supported bases, then resubmit the complete active set in one validation call. The server commits only active answers.

Apply every reported repair and retain other drafted answers. Add missing questions to the existing answer set. Resolve further activation from the repaired answers before resubmitting. The server ignores inactive answers.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

Availability and mitigation are separate premises: a familiar method name or numerically stable estimate is not enough; the sensitivity analysis must span plausible assumptions relevant to the documented missingness mechanism.
This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.

considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation is not loss to follow-up when outcome ascertainment continues; stopping treatment or an analysis label alone does not establish whether the outcome was observed. Last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.

Withdrawal or censoring after worsening health or symptoms can support possible dependence on the outcome value when the source links the reason to that participant's outcome; stopping treatment without that follow-up loss does not.

Randomisation and masking
Randomisation was done by a clinical research organ-
isation and was centralised nationally. Patients were
randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to receive ADT plus
docetaxel or ADT alone. Dynamic minimisation was
used to minimise the imbalance of three criteria:
previous systemic treatment with ADT; chemotherapy
for local disease or isolated rising PSA; and Glass risk
groups.8 Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not
masked to treatment allocation.

Methods In this randomised, open-label, phase 3 study, we enrolled patients in 29 centres in France and one in
Belgium. Eligible patients were older than 18 years and had histologically confi rmed adenocarcinoma of the prostate
and radiologically proven metastatic disease; a Karnofsky score of at least 70%; a life expectancy of at least 3 months;
and adequate hepatic, haematological, and renal function. They were randomly assigned to receive to ADT (orchiectomy
or luteinising hormone-releasing hormone agonists, alone or combined with non-steroidal antiandrogens) alone or in
combination with docetaxel (75 mg/m2 intravenously on the fi rst day of each 21-day cycle; up to nine cycles). Patients
were randomised in a 1:1 ratio, with dynamic minimisation to minimise imbalances in previous systemic treatment
with ADT, chemotherapy for local disease or isolated rising concentration of serum prostate-specifi c antigen, and
Glass risk groups. Patients, physicians, and data analysts were not masked to treatment allocation. The primary
endpoint was overall survival. Effi cacy analyses were done by intention to treat. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.
gov, number NCT00104715.

questions.wording: Was the method of measuring the outcome inappropriate?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’ if the method of measuring the outcome is inappropriate, for example because it is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the measurement instrument has been demonstrated to have poor validity.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 54, Box 10, signalling question 4.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate for the outcome, including validity and sensitivity to plausible intervention effects.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when the method is unlikely to be sensitive to plausible intervention effects or the instrument has demonstrated poor validity. Validity and sensitivity are distinct from detection opportunity, assessor identity or awareness, and whether knowledge influenced assessment. Do not assess whether choosing the outcome itself was sensible.
evidence_needed: The measurement method's sensitivity to plausible effects and evidence of instrument validity for this outcome.

For a mixed objective and subjective composite, inspect each component that can determine the approved event; objective components do not establish validity or influence conclusions for a subjective component.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when appropriateness of the measurement method cannot be determined.

answer_anchors.text: The measurement method is unsuitable, insensitive, or poorly valid for this outcome.
The measurement method is appropriate for this outcome.

considerations: For pre-specified outcomes the answer will usually be no or probably no.

Measurement susceptibility concerns whether the method can validly and sensitively measure this outcome. It is distinct from assessor awareness, detection opportunity, and whether knowledge of intervention likely influenced assessment.

A standardized instrument can still involve judgment in elicitation, attribution, grading, or assessment. Preserve component-specific Evidence and uncertainty for mixed objective and subjective components.

evidence.quote:
We assessed clinical history, weight, and Karnofsky
performance status, and did a physical examination
before treatment began. We did a CT scan, a bone scan,
electrocardiography, and blood tests (including meas ure-
ment of serum PSA) within 30 days before initiation of
treatment. We repeated physical examinations and blood
tests every 3 weeks during treatment in the group given
ADT plus docetaxel and every 3 months in the group
given ADT alone. We did imaging studies every 3 months;
radiological response was to be confi rmed within
4 weeks. After 42 months, we did clinical, labora tory, and
radiological examinations every 6 months.
The primary endpoint was overall survival (ie, time
between randomisation and death from any cause).
Secondary endpoints were time to clinical progression or
death (clinical progression-free survival; cPFS) and time
to PSA progression, clinical progression, or death
(biochemical progression-free survival; bPFS).
We defi ned biochemical progression with the PSA
Working Group defi nition:11 a previous confi rmed PSA
decrease of at least 50% and an increase of at least 50%
above the nadir, with a minimum increase of 5 ng/mL.
For patients without a previous PSA decrease of 50%,
progression was defi ned as a PSA increase of at least
25% above the nadir and of at least 5 ng/mL.
A confi rmatory PSA test was mandatory in all cases.
In patients with measurable lesions, we defi ned clinical
progression as the progression of pre-existing lesions
with Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors
(RECIST; version 1.0)12 or the occurrence of (new) bone
lesions, whichever happened fi rst. In patients with only
bone lesions, progression was defi ned as one or more
new bone lesions on bone scan or occurrence of a new
soft-tissue lesion, whichever happened fi rst. Death was
judged as an event; causes of deaths were reported by
investigators rather than by central review.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.

questions.bias_construct: Whether measurement or ascertainment of the outcome could have differed between intervention groups.
considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Tie every monitoring difference to the approved event. Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. Treatment duration, median progression-free survival, or a treatment-emergent label alone does not establish when or how adverse events were observed.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.
questions.decision_rule: Comparable measurement uses the same methods and thresholds at comparable time points. Consider diagnostic detection bias from passive collection and additional healthcare visits caused by an intervention, but identify the pathway by which a different detection opportunity could change ascertainment before judging its severity.
evidence_needed: Methods, thresholds, timing, and opportunities for outcome ascertainment in each intervention group, plus the pathway connecting any opportunity difference to differential detection.
